summary.title: Tutorial: Using CamShift to Track Objects in Video
summary.one_liner: You learn to track a user-selected object in video with OpenCV's CamShift, using a hue-histogram back projection and a four-point bounding box selected with the mouse.
takeaways: CamShift tracks an object by back-projecting a reference hue histogram onto each HSV frame and iterating to find the object's new position.
The ROI is picked by clicking four points with the mouse, then pressing 'i' to enter selection mode; the code derives a top-left and bottom-right box from them.
The termination criteria cap CamShift at 10 iterations or a one-pixel centroid change to keep the tracker near real-time.
Limitations: only the Hue channel is used, histogram bin count needs tuning, and OpenCV (at the time) did not support 3D histograms in back projection.
For more robust tracking with texture and local features, the author suggests keypoint detection, SIFT/DoG descriptors and homographies.
summary.summary: Adrian Rosebrock's PyImageSearch tutorial walks through a Python script (track.py) that uses OpenCV's cv2.CamShift to track an object in a webcam or video file. The user selects four points around the object with the mouse, the script builds a 16-bin hue histogram from that region, and then back-projects it onto each HSV frame to follow the object. The post explains each code block line by line and discusses limitations such as hue-only tracking and bin tuning, and points to keypoint-based methods as a more robust alternative.
